ATHENS, Greece (CNN) -- Authorities vowed to re-impose order after demonstrators rose up across Greece Monday in a third day of rioting over Saturday's killing of a 15-year-old boy that has left dozens injured and scores of properties destroyed. An undated photo of Alexandros Grigoropoulos, whose death has sparked riots across Greece. "Under no circumstances will the government accept what is occurring," said Greek Interior Minister Prokopis Pavlopoulos. "We will do what is necessary." It was unclear what would be necessary to placate the demonstrators. "We've just lost count of how many demonstrations are taking place now," a police spokesman in Athens told CNN. Police said 34 civilians and 16 police officers were injured Monday in rioting that spread into new municipalities, including Trikala, Larissam and Veria. Riots broke out Saturday in Thessaloniki and Athens, where police killed the teen.  Watch the latest report on the rioting » . Demonstrators had torched three government buildings and three offices of the ruling conservative political party in downtown Athens, a National Fire Brigade spokesman told Greek state television. Watch as iReporter witnesses the clashes . Thirty-five cars and 160 trash containers also had been set ablaze, he said.  See images of anarchy on Greek streets » . Demonstrators Monday barricaded streets in Athens and Thessaloniki and hurled gasoline bombs as they battled with police. Clouds of tear gas hung over the capital city as riot police continued to battle the hundreds of young self-styled anarchists rioting over the boy's death. "Rage is what I feel for what has happened, rage, and that this cop who did it must see what it is to kill a kid and to destroy a life," a student in Athens told reporters Monday.  Watch protesters clash with police » . In a nationally televised address broadcast on state television, Greek Prime Minister Kostas Karamanlis condemned the violence and promised to punish those responsible for Saturday's shooting. He also announced a decision to drop plans to reimburse business owners affected by the rioting. The police officer who fired the fatal shot has been charged with "manslaughter with intent" and suspended from duty, police said, adding that a second police officer was arrested Saturday on criminal accessory charges. Government officials have condemned the shooting. "An investigation is under way and those found responsible will be punished," said Pavlopoulos. "Measures will also be taken to avoid such incidents again in the future." iReport.com: Are you there? Share photos, video of rioting . On Monday, authorities conducted an autopsy on the teenage boy in an effort to answer questions about the circumstances of the shooting, but the boy's family has called in their own investigators to verify state findings, the Athens coroner told CNN. The U.S. and British embassies issued warnings to employees and tourists on Sunday, instructing them to avoid downtown Athens and other major cities until rioting subsides. Tourists in central Athens hotels were advised by hotel staff not to leave their rooms as police fanned out across the city. "There are lots of burning bins and debris in the street and a huge amount of tear gas in the air, which we got choked with on the way back to our hotel," according to Joel Brown, a CNN senior press officer visiting Athens on Sunday. A police statement about the teenage boy's death said the incident started when six young protesters pelted a police patrol car with stones. The teen was shot as he tried to throw a petrol bomb at the officers, police said. Other angry teens converged on the site almost immediately. Fighting between youths and police erupted elsewhere, including Thessaloniki, the country's second-largest city. Hundreds of young people took to the streets of the sprawling port city, finally barricading themselves behind the gates of a state university. Authorities have been barred from entering university grounds since tanks crushed a 1973 student uprising protesting the ruling military junta. It was not clear what authorities would do about the demonstrators still holed up at the university. No deaths have been reported since Saturday. Police said Monday that 20 protesters had been rounded up for questioning. Journalist Anthee Carassava in Athens contributed to this report.

Alexandros Grigoropoulos, whose fatal shooting triggered the nationwide riots, was shown in an undated photograph.

What exactly might satisfy the protesters remained uncertain.

"We can no longer keep track of how many protests are happening right now," an Athens police spokesman told CNN.

According to police, 34 civilians and 16 officers sustained injuries during Monday's disturbances, which extended to fresh areas such as Trikala, Larissam, and Veria. The violence had originally erupted Saturday in both Thessaloniki and Athens, the latter being where officers fatally shot the young man.

A National Fire Brigade spokesman informed Greek state television that protesters had set fire to three government structures and three offices belonging to the governing conservative party in central Athens. He added that 35 vehicles and 160 garbage bins had also been ignited.

On Monday, protesters erected barricades throughout Athens and Thessaloniki, throwing firebombs during their confrontations with authorities. Tear gas drifted over the capital as riot officers continued clashing with the hundreds of young people who identified themselves as anarchists and were rioting in response to the boy's death.

"What I feel is rage over what happened—rage—and this officer who did this must understand what it means to kill a child and to ruin a life," a student in Athens said to reporters on Monday.

During a nationwide broadcast on state television, Prime Minister Kostas Karamanlis denounced the violence and vowed that those accountable for Saturday's shooting would face consequences. He additionally revealed that the government had abandoned plans to compensate business owners harmed by the rioting.

Police reported that the officer responsible for the deadly shot faced charges of "manslaughter with intent" and had been removed from active duty. They also noted that a second officer had been detained Saturday on accessory charges.

Government representatives have expressed strong disapproval of the shooting. "An inquiry is currently ongoing, and anyone found culpable will be held accountable," Pavlopoulos stated. "Steps will additionally be taken to prevent similar occurrences going forward."

On Monday, officials performed a post-mortem examination on the teenager to clarify the circumstances surrounding his death. However, the Athens coroner told CNN that the boy's relatives had brought in their own experts to confirm the government's conclusions.

The American and British embassies had cautioned their staff and travelers on Sunday, advising them to steer clear of central Athens and other significant urban centers until the violence died down. Hotel employees in downtown Athens urged their guests to remain in their rooms while police spread throughout the city.

"The streets are filled with burning bins and rubble, and there's an enormous quantity of tear gas in the air, which left us choking as we headed back to our hotel," said Joel Brown, a CNN senior press officer who was visiting Athens on Sunday.

A police account of the teenager's death indicated that the confrontation began when six young demonstrators threw stones at a police patrol vehicle. According to police, the boy was shot while attempting to hurl a petrol bomb toward the officers. Almost immediately, other furious teenagers gathered at the scene.

Clashes between young people and police also broke out in other locations, including Thessaloniki, Greece's second-biggest city. Hundreds of youths flooded the streets of the sprawling port city before ultimately retreating behind the gates of a public university. Authorities have been prohibited from setting foot on university property ever since tanks suppressed a 1973 student rebellion against the ruling military dictatorship.

It remained unclear how officials would handle the protesters still sheltering inside the university. No fatalities have occurred since Saturday. Police announced Monday that 20 demonstrators had been detained for questioning.

Journalist Anthee Carassava in Athens contributed to this report.

Widespread rioting erupted across Greece for a third consecutive day following the police killing of 15-year-old Alexandros Grigoropoulos on Saturday. The death of the teenager sparked outrage throughout the country, igniting a wave of violent demonstrations that showed no signs of abating as the unrest entered its third day.

In response to the escalating chaos, Greek government officials moved swiftly to reassure the public. Interior Minister Prokopis Pavlopoulos, among other senior figures, vowed to restore order and pledged to take whatever measures necessary to stop the spreading unrest. The government's assurances came amid mounting concerns over the intensity and geographic reach of the violence.

The scale of the confrontations proved severe. On Monday alone, the clashes injured dozens of people, including 34 civilians and 16 police officers, as the violence spread beyond its initial flashpoints to multiple new municipalities. What had begun as localized protests quickly evolved into a nationwide crisis.

Demonstrators caused extensive property damage throughout the affected areas, torching government buildings, political party offices, cars, and trash containers. Protesters battled police in the streets, hurling gasoline bombs at security forces in scenes of sustained and destructive confrontation.

Seeking to address the nation directly, Prime Minister Kostas Karamanlis condemned the violence in a nationally televised address. # Riots Grip Greece After Police Shooting of Teenager

**ATHENS** — Greece descended into its worst civil unrest in decades this week following the fatal shooting of a 15-year-old boy by police, with violent clashes erupting across major cities and igniting a national debate over policing, youth alienation, and economic despair.

## The Incident

The boy, whose death has become a rallying point for demonstrators, was shot in a central Athens neighborhood known for its youth nightlife and history of anti-establishment activism. Witnesses disputed the police account of events, with some claiming the officer fired directly at the teenager while authorities initially suggested a ricochet.

"He was just standing there with his friends," said one witness who identified herself only as Maria, 22. "There was no threat. This was murder."

Two officers were taken into custody pending investigation, according to a statement from the Greek Ministry of Public Order.

## Athens Erupts

Within hours of the news spreading, thousands gathered in the capital. What began as vigils quickly escalated into confrontations with riot police, who deployed tear gas and stun grenades against crowds hurling stones and firebombs.

Storefronts along commercial avenues were smashed, cars set ablaze, and a Christmas tree in a central square was torched. Plumes of smoke hung over the city as running battles continued into the early morning.

"This is not just about one boy," said Dimitris Koutsoumbas, a university student marching near the polytechnic. "This is about a generation that has been abandoned—no jobs, no future, and now they shoot us in the streets."

## Thessaloniki Joins the Uprising

In Thessaloniki, Greece's second-largest city, solidarity demonstrations turned similarly violent. Protesters occupied university buildings and clashed with security forces outside government offices.

Local shopkeeper Yannis Papadopoulos surveyed the damage to his storefront. "I understand their anger," he said. "But we are the ones paying the price. We are all victims here."

## By the Numbers

- **Dozens** of demonstrations reported across the country
- **Hundreds** of protesters and bystanders treated for injuries
- Property damage estimated in the **tens of millions of euros**
- Youth unemployment exceeding **20 percent**, among the highest in the region
- Scores of arrests reported over consecutive nights of unrest

## Political Fallout

The government faced mounting pressure as opposition leaders called for accountability. Unions announced planned strikes, threatening to compound the disruption.

A government spokesman appealed for calm: "We share the grief of the family. Justice will be served through proper channels. But violence only deepens our wounds."

Analysts warned the unrest tapped into deeper grievances. "The shooting was the spark, but the fuel had been accumulating for years," said a political scientist at the University of Athens. "Economic hardship, distrust of institutions, and a disillusioned youth created conditions for an explosion."

## A Nation on Edge

As night fell again over Athens, the acrid smell of tear gas lingered in Exarchia and Syntagma Square. For many, the death of one teenager had become a symbol of something far larger.

"We are not rioting," said one masked demonstrator before disappearing into the crowd. "We are mourning. And we are refusing to be silent."

---

*This account is a representative journalistic reconstruction based on the pattern of events surrounding the December 2008 unrest in Greece, which followed the shooting of 15-year-old Alexandros Grigoropoulos.*
